title: Leaders Can Always Make a Bad Decision Worse
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Borrowing Tom Kite's definition of a double bogey as "a bad shot followed by a stupid shot," the piece argues that the real danger after a bad decision is compounding it with a worse one. The authors identify two causes: leaders are distracted by the earlier misstep and not thinking clearly, or they gamble on a risky move to recover. Underneath both is the need to redeem oneself and regain lost credibility, which pushes leaders to swing for the fences. Occasional bad decisions are inevitable, but following one with an idiotic choice reflects a lack of discipline. The prescription is to stay vigilant, slow down, regain composure and hold the standard that the next decision must not compound the problem. Like a golfer taking a bogey and moving on, leaders should accept the cost of the first mistake rather than chase it.
points: The double bogey analogy reframes mistakes: the first bad shot is forgivable, the follow-up stupid shot is the real failure of discipline.
Compounding errors usually stem from distraction after the misstep or from risky attempts to recover lost ground.
The urge to redeem credibility after a visible mistake is the main driver of a worse second decision.
Simply knowing the tendency to take unnecessary risks after a poor decision helps leaders slow down and choose well.
Adopt an explicit standard: the next decision must not compound the problem; take the bogey and move on.
quotes: Decision-makers who follow a bad decision with an equally bad choice — or worse — usually do so for one of two reasons. They are distracted by the earlier misstep and are not thinking clearly, or they are attempting to recover by making a risky move that will likely end up in disaster.
Making a bad decision on occasion is inevitable. Compounding a bad decision by following it with an idiotic choice reflects a lack of discipline.
Swinging for the fences or taking risks to recover is almost always a bad choice. Regaining the composure to make a quality decision is essential. The main problem is our need to recover.

When leaders or decision-makers make a mistake, especially one that is seen as a bad decision by others, they feel a need to redeem themselves. They put all of their energy into the next decision, often in an attempt to regain the credibility or advantage that has already been squandered.
The best leaders know this all too well and maintain the discipline to slow down, take a deep breath, and focus on making a quality follow-up decision that does not compound the problem.
Holding the standard that the next decision must not compound the problem will usually prevent a calamity.
